statement: In people taking part in the same 572 case–control and cohort studies (Bagnardi et al., 2015), light drinking (up to 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average, one drink or less as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers not separated) is associated with slightly more of some cancers and slightly fewer of others, with no absolute risks reported: pooled relative risks of 1.13 (95% CI 1.00–1.26) for cancers of the mouth and pharynx (52 studies), 1.26 (1.06–1.50) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (54 studies), 1.04 (1.01–1.07) for female breast cancer (115 studies, editors' count) and 1.04 (1.01–1.08) for prostate cancer; no clear difference for cancers of the colon and rectum (0.99, 0.95–1.04), liver (1.00, 0.85–1.18) or larynx (0.87, 0.68–1.11); and lower figures for lung cancer (0.84, 0.79–0.88), oesophageal adenocarcinoma with gastric cardia (0.86, 0.76–0.98), cancers of the kidney (0.92, 0.86–0.99) and thyroid (0.81, 0.74–0.88), and both kinds of lymphoma (Hodgkin's 0.73, 0.59–0.89; non-Hodgkin's 0.88, 0.80–0.97). Differences this small can be produced or hidden by people who drink more reporting less, which the authors say may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations, by smoking and other differences (only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates), and by former or occasional drinkers among the comparison group; the raised figures for the mouth and pharynx and the oesophagus were statistically clear only in Asian studies (1.33 and 1.54), and the lower lung and oesophageal adenocarcinoma figures appear in the review's figure but not in its text. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, drawing on an overlapping set of studies, fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer (Griswold et al., 2018), and a model of cancers in 2020 attributes 41,300 new cases worldwide (95% uncertainty interval 35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, against lifetime abstention (Rumgay et al., 2021); both depend on the shape of the risk curves at low intake, which is what these studies leave uncertain. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In the same studies, people who had up to about one drink a day (12.5 g of alcohol) had slightly more mouth and throat cancer (1.13 times, a borderline result), one type of gullet cancer (1.26 times), breast cancer (1.04 times) and prostate cancer (1.04 times) than people who did not drink, and slightly less lung, kidney and thyroid cancer and cancer of the lymph glands. The review gives no numbers out of 100. Differences this small could come from people who drink more saying they drink less, from smoking and other differences, or from people who had stopped drinking being counted with people who did not drink. A model of cancers worldwide counted 41,300 new cancers in 2020 from drinking up to 10 g a day, compared with no one ever drinking; that figure depends on the shape of the risk curves at low amounts, which is what these studies leave uncertain.
population: People in 572 case–control and cohort studies published 1956 to 2012 (486,538 people with cancer), mostly from North America, Europe and Asia
exposure: Light drinking: average intake up to 12.5 g of ethanol a day (up to one drink as the review defines it), self-reported
comparator: Nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers not separated
outcome: Incidence of, or death from, cancer at 23 sites
magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, light drinking against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers (pooled RR, 95% CI; I²): mouth and pharynx 1.13 (1.00–1.26; 26%); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.26 (1.06–1.50; 68%); female breast 1.04 (1.01–1.07; 63%); prostate 1.04 (1.01–1.08); colon and rectum 0.99 (0.95–1.04); liver 1.00 (0.85–1.18); larynx 0.87 (0.68–1.11); lung 0.84 (0.79–0.88); oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76–0.98); kidney 0.92 (0.86–0.99); thyroid 0.81 (0.74–0.88); Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.73 (0.59–0.89); non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.88 (0.80–0.97). Asian studies only: mouth and pharynx 1.33 (1.06–1.68; 7 studies), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.54 (1.18–2.00; 11 studies). Rumgay et al. 2021 (model): 41,300 (35,400–145,800) new cancers in 2020 attributed to intake up to 10 g a day against lifetime abstention.

risk_of_bias.note: As for the moderate and heavy estimates (card sc_bagnardi_2015: AMSTAR 2 critically low), and at light intake the biases are as large as the associations: under-reporting moves people who drink more into the light category, former and occasional drinkers in the reference group can move the estimates either way, and about half the estimates are crude; the authors concede that under-reporting may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations.

inconsistency.note: Positive associations at some sites and inverse ones at others (lung, oesophageal adenocarcinoma, kidney, thyroid, lymphomas); by region the oral and oesophageal associations were clear only in Asian studies, and prostate and melanoma only in North American ones; I² 26% to 68% for the positive estimates; no adequate explanation.

indirectness.note: Light drinking as the studies classed it (midpoint up to 12.5 g a day), in the populations studied.

imprecision.note: The breast estimate is precise (1.01–1.07); the interval for the mouth and pharynx reaches 1.00; not rated down separately, the certainty being already at the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not examined in the review; small light-drinking effects are the kind most open to selective publication; stated rather than rated, the certainty being already at the floor.

dose_response.note: Not applied: whether the gradient seen at higher intake continues to the lowest intakes is the question this claim addresses, and the biases are largest there.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down one level each for risk of bias and inconsistency, which is below the floor, so very low. Rated as worded: small associations in both directions at light intake, site by site; with these data none can be told apart from bias. The Global Burden of Disease curves draw largely on the same studies, and the 2020 model's low-intake figure rests on the shape of its curves at low intake, so neither is independent support. Status mixed: findings differ by site and by region without an adequate explanation.
